# What the letters mean {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c l l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Letter & Unit & Unit symbol & Simple meaning\\
\midrule
Current & $I$ & ampere & A & How much electric charge is moving.\\
Voltage & $V$ & volt & V & The electrical push across two points.\\
Resistance & $R$ & ohm & $\Omega$ & How strongly a part limits current.\\
Power & $P$ & watt & W & How quickly electrical energy is used.\\
Energy & $E$ & joule & J & How much work it can do or has already done.\\
Charge & $Q$ & coulomb & C & The amount of electric charge.\\
Time & $t$ & second & s & How long something happens.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{Why is current written as $I$?} $I$ means current. It comes from the older phrase \textit{current intensity}.
```

# Significant figures {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}p{0.24\textwidth} Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Situation & What to do\\
\midrule
Multiply or divide & Use the fewest significant figures in the question.\\
Add or subtract & Use the fewest decimal places in the question.\\
During the calculation & Keep the full calculator value.\\
Final answer & Round once. Include the metric prefix and unit.\\
Prefix and unit & Use a prefix so the number is from 0 to 999. Example: $0.047\ \mathrm{A}=47\ \mathrm{mA}$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\section*{Common metric prefixes}
\textbf{Write the number, metric prefix, and unit together.} Example: $4700\ \Omega=4.7\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$.

\begin{center}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.18}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Prefix & Symbol & Power & Example\\
\midrule
giga & G & $10^9$ & $2.4\ \mathrm{GHz}$\\
mega & M & $10^6$ & $3.3\ \mathrm{M}\Omega$\\
kilo & k & $10^3$ & $4.7\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$\\
no prefix & none & $10^0$ & $12\ \mathrm{V}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Prefix & Symbol & Power & Example\\
\midrule
milli & m & $10^{-3}$ & $47\ \mathrm{mA}$\\
micro & $\mu$ & $10^{-6}$ & $220\ \mu\mathrm{F}$\\
nano & n & $10^{-9}$ & $100\ \mathrm{nF}$\\
pico & p & $10^{-12}$ & $22\ \mathrm{pF}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}
\end{center}
```

# GUESS method {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries\large}c l Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Letter & Step & What to write\\
\midrule
G & Given & List the known symbols, values, and units in a table.\\
U & Unknown & List what you need to find and its unit.\\
E & Equation & Write the general equation, then rearrange it.\\
S & Substitute & Put the numbers and units into the equation.\\
S & Solve & Calculate, round once, include the metric prefix and unit, and write an answer sentence.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
```

\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\section*{Ohm's law}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.75}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Find & Formula & Units\\
\midrule
Voltage & $V=I\times R$ & volts (V)\\
Current & $\displaystyle I=\frac{V}{R}$ & amperes (A)\\[16pt]
Resistance & $\displaystyle R=\frac{V}{I}$ & ohms ($\Omega$)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{minipage}\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.48\textwidth}
\section*{Power and energy}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.65}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Use when you know & Formula & Unit\\
\midrule
Voltage and current & $P=V\times I$ & W\\
Current and resistance & $P=I^2\times R$ & W\\[12pt]
Voltage and resistance & $\displaystyle P=\frac{V^2}{R}$ & W\\[12pt]
Power and time & $E=P\times t$ & J\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{minipage}

\textbf{Choose the equation that uses the values known in the problem.}

\section*{General equations and specific values}
\begin{tejnote}[What a subscript does]
A plain letter such as $V$, $I$, $R$, or $P$ names a general quantity. A subscript identifies the total circuit, a particular component, or a particular branch.
\end{tejnote}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.60}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Type of value & Example equation & Meaning\\
\midrule
General & $\displaystyle R=\frac{V}{I}$ & The relationship works for any resistance, voltage, and current.\\[18pt]
Total circuit & $\displaystyle R_T=\frac{V_T}{I_T}$ & Every value belongs to the whole circuit.\\[18pt]
Part or branch 1 & $\displaystyle R_1=\frac{V_1}{I_1}$ & Every value belongs to component or branch 1.\\[18pt]
Part or branch 2 & $P_2=V_2\times I_2$ & Every value belongs to component or branch 2.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{Keep subscripts together:} If you are calculating part 1, use the values marked with subscript 1.

\section*{How the subscripts change the meaning}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.30}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Subscript & Examples & Meaning\\
\midrule
None & $I$, $V$, $R$, $P$ & A general quantity in an equation. It does not identify a particular branch.\\
$T$ & $I_T$, $V_T$, $R_T$, $P_T$ & The total value for the whole circuit.\\
$1$, $2$, and so on & $I_1$, $V_1$, $R_1$, $P_1$ & The value for a numbered branch or component.\\
$S$ & $V_S$ & The source voltage. In this simple circuit, $V_S=V_T$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{In a parallel circuit:} $I_1$ and $I_2$ are branch currents. $V_1$ and $V_2$ are the voltages across branches 1 and 2.

\section*{Parallel rules}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.55}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Rule & Meaning\\
\midrule
Voltage & $V_T=V_1=V_2=\cdots$ & Voltage is the same across every branch.\\
Current & $I_T=I_1+I_2+\cdots$ & Add the branch currents.\\
Resistance & $\dfrac{1}{R_T}=\dfrac{1}{R_1}+\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\cdots$ & Add the reciprocals.\\[22pt]
Two resistors & $R_T=\dfrac{R_1\times R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ & Use this shortcut for two resistors.\\[14pt]
Power & $P_T=P_1+P_2+\cdots$ & Add the branch powers.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{Quick check:} $R_T$ is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

\clearpage
\thispagestyle{fancy}
\vspace*{0.32in}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c}
{\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} Series Circuits}\\[3pt]
{\normalsize One path through every component}
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=white,colframe=black,boxrule=1pt,arc=0mm,left=2mm,right=2mm,top=1.5mm,bottom=1.5mm]
\centering\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} ONE PATH. SAME CURRENT THROUGH EVERY PART.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{center}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{../schematics/bw/Series_Rule_Reference.pdf}
\end{center}

\section*{How the subscripts change the meaning}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.30}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Subscript & Examples & Meaning\\
\midrule
None & $I$, $V$, $R$, $P$ & A general quantity in an equation. It does not identify a particular part.\\
$T$ & $I_T$, $V_T$, $R_T$, $P_T$ & The total value for the whole circuit.\\
$1$, $2$, and so on & $I_1$, $V_1$, $R_1$, $P_1$ & The value for a numbered component or location.\\
$S$ & $V_S$ & The source voltage. In this simple circuit, $V_S=V_T$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\textbf{In a series circuit:} $I_1$ and $I_2$ are the currents through components 1 and 2. $V_1$ and $V_2$ are the voltage drops across those components.

\section*{Series rules}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.40}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Quantity & Rule & Meaning\\
\midrule
Current & $I_T=I_1=I_2=\cdots$ & Current is the same through every part.\\
Voltage & $V_T=V_1+V_2+\cdots$ & Add the voltage drops.\\
Resistance & $R_T=R_1+R_2+\cdots$ & Add the component resistances.\\
Power & $P_T=P_1+P_2+\cdots$ & Add the component powers.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

{\Large\bfseries\color{TEJNavy} Series Summation Notation}\\[3pt]
{\normalsize The sigma symbol means add a sequence of values}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{circuitikz}[scale=1.05,transform shape]
  \draw (0,0)
    to[battery1,l=$V_S$] (0,2)

\textbf{Three resistors in one path are added to find the total resistance.}
\end{center}

\section*{Summation notation}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.55}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{>{\bfseries}l c Y}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TEJMist}
Case & Equation & Meaning\\
\midrule
Any number & $\displaystyle R_T=\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_i=R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_n$ & Start at resistor 1 and add every resistor through resistor $n$.\\[20pt]
Three resistors & $\displaystyle R_T=\sum_{i=1}^{3}R_i=R_1+R_2+R_3$ & The 1 is where counting starts. The 3 is where counting stops.\\[20pt]
Example & $R_T=100\ \Omega+220\ \Omega+330\ \Omega=650\ \Omega$ & Three series resistors have a total resistance of $650\ \Omega$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\begin{tejnote}[Capital letters matter]
$M$ means mega, but $m$ means milli. On the calculator, $1.0\mathrm{E}6$ means $1.0\times10^6$.
\end{tejnote}
